strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-motivated: it identifies ill-conditioned gradient spectra as a candidate mechanism for grokking plateaus, and the toy linear-model analysis (Theorem 1, Corollary 1) is clean, self-contained, and analytically verified against experiments (Figure 6).

The proposed EGD update is simple and elegant: whitening the layer gradient via (GG^T)^{-1/2} preserves singular directions while equalizing singular values, and its connections to natural gradient (Eq. 13) and Grokfast (Eq. 14) are insightful and help position the method conceptually.

The empirical results are striking: on modular addition/multiplication and sparse parity, EGD removes plateaus that persist for thousands of epochs under vanilla SGD, and the simplified column-normalization variant also works, suggesting the effect is robust.
The method is advertised as hyperparameter-free and drop-in, with a Fisher-norm constant-of-motion analysis providing some theoretical grounding for the nonlinear case.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: per-layer gradient whitening/preconditioning with (GG^T)^{-1/2} or related matrices is well studied in the natural gradient, K-FAC, Shampoo, and spectral-normalization literatures. The paper's contribution is essentially applying a known preconditioner to grokking; the framing as a 'novel' method overstates the delta.

The 'effective theory' is confined to a 2D linear model with quadratic loss. There is no theory for the nonlinear networks actually used in experiments; the causal link between ill-conditioned gradients (Figure 4) and grokking in MLPs remains correlational. The jump from Insight #1 (linear toy) to the claim that EGD 'provably' accelerates grokking in general is not supported.

Critical baseline comparisons are missing: Grokfast is discussed at length (Section 4.2) as the main related method, yet is never run as a baseline, nor are Adam or other known grokking accelerators (weight decay tuning, learning-rate warmup of Lyle et al.). Without these, the claimed advantages (memory, simplicity, theory) are not empirically validated.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only small 2-layer MLPs on algorithmic tasks. No transformers, no naturalistic settings, no results on tasks where EGD might hurt (e.g., due to whitening distorting gradient geometry). The claim 'without compromising final generalization' is asserted but only weakly supported.

Practical cost is significant and under-addressed: a full SVD of every layer's gradient matrix at every step is expensive; the mitigation (switch off EGD once grokking is detected via validation loss) makes the method depend on detection heuristics, which somewhat undercuts the 'hyperparameter-free, drop-in' claim. The reported use of LR=0.7 for modular arithmetic also raises fairness questions about hyperparameter tuning across methods.

Reproducibility and rigor concerns: no error bars, seeds, or number of runs reported; several typos and inconsistencies ('EGT' in Figure 4 caption, lowercase 'warm-up' section heading, garbled Table 1 layout); the abstract/intro claims are stronger than the evidence (e.g., 'stagnation is completely removed' is shown only on small algorithmic tasks).

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a clean narrative from toy theory to a practical method to experiments.
The toy linear model yields an analytic characterization of grokking (Theorem 1, Corollary 1), and Figure 6 shows the theory matches simulations well, which is a nice pedagogical result.

The proposed method (EGD) is simple, hyperparameter-free, and the empirical results on modular arithmetic and sparse parity do show plateaus being removed or drastically shortened relative to vanilla SGD.
The connection drawn to natural gradient descent (Eq. 13) and to the filtering behavior of Grokfast (Eq. 14) is conceptually interesting and places the method in context.
Hyperparameters for all experiments are reported in Appendix B, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: per-layer whitening/rescaling of gradient matrices so that singular values are equalized is essentially known in the optimization literature (e.g., natural gradient variants, spectral/SVD-based updates such as spectral descent, Shampoo/MMuon-style methods, spectral normalization). The paper's own analysis shows EGD is a 'whitened version of NGD'. The main new element is applying it to grokking, which is an incremental contribution.

Theory is confined to a 2-dimensional linear toy model. The central mechanistic claim — that grokking is 'sole due to delayed convergence of the least-squares solution caused by ill-conditioned gradients' (Insight #1) — is far too strong given the evidence, and it is not reconciled with competing explanations in the literature (weight-decay/norm effects, circuit competition, kernel-to-rich escape). Notably, the theory has no weight decay, yet all neural network experiments use weight decay, which is widely considered essential for grokking to occur at all.

Experimental evaluation is narrow: only 2-layer ReLU MLPs on toy algorithmic tasks. The standard grokking benchmark (small transformers on modular arithmetic) is absent, and no tasks 'beyond algorithmic' are tested, so the generality claims in the abstract and conclusion are unsupported.

Missing key baselines and comparisons: the paper extensively discusses Grokfast (Section 4.2) claiming advantages, but never runs it head-to-head. Adam and other whitening-based optimizers (Muon, Shampoo, K-FAC) are also absent, and these are the natural competitors for an optimization-side intervention.

Potential confound in comparisons: EGD produces gradients with (nearly) unit singular values, so per-step update norms are much larger than vanilla SGD's; the improvement may simply reflect an effective learning-rate/norm effect rather than 'egalitarianization' of the spectrum. Column Normalization partially controls for this, but no experiment disentangles normalization of update magnitude from spectral equalization (e.g., norm-matched SGD baselines).

Computational cost is unaddressed: full SVD of every layer's gradient matrix per step is expensive, yet no wall-clock/runtime comparison or overhead measurement is reported. The workaround of switching EGD off after detecting grokking via validation monitoring is a heuristic that further complicates fair evaluation.
No statistical rigor: no seeds, error bars, or variance analysis are reported; several figures show single runs with visible variability (e.g., Figure 3).

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and important details (e.g., the randomized SVD approximation claimed to 'work just fine', how grokking detection via validation loss is implemented) are asserted without evidence or specification.

Presentation issues undermine polish: Section 3 heading is lowercase ('warm-up'), the Figure 4 caption says 'EGT' instead of EGD, the conclusion uses 'Equalitarian' vs. 'Egalitarian', and there are multiple typos ('gradients descen', 'gradient decent', a sentence fragment on page 8 about replacing columns of G).

strengths: The proposed EGD method is simple, hyperparameter-free, and well-motivated: equalizing singular values of the layer gradient matrix is an elegant and clearly articulated idea.

The toy linear-model analysis (Section 3, Theorem 1, Corollary 1) is clean and analytically tractable, and the closed-form theory matches the experimental curves in Figure 6, giving a genuine mechanistic account of plateau formation via ill-conditioned gradient spectra.

The connections drawn to natural gradient descent (whitened NGD, Eq. 13) and to Grokfast's low-pass filtering (Section 4.2) are insightful and situate the method within existing acceleration approaches.

Empirical results on standard grokking benchmarks (modular addition/multiplication, sparse parity) show dramatic plateau removal, which is a striking and reproducible-looking phenomenon across multiple problem sizes.
weaknesses: Limited empirical scope: all experiments are on small 2-layer ReLU networks solving algorithmic tasks. There are no transformer experiments, no larger/naturalistic tasks, and the claim that EGD 'eliminates the plateaus' in general is stronger than the evidence provided.

Missing key baselines: despite an extensive discussion of Grokfast, the paper never compares against it empirically; comparisons to Adam, weight-decay tuning, or other recent acceleration methods (e.g., Prieto et al. 2025, Grokalign) are also absent, so it is unclear whether EGD offers practical advantages over existing, cheaper accelerators.

The 'Column Normalization' baseline performs nearly as well as full EGD in several plots (e.g., Fig. 1 p=97, Fig. 3 k=3/k=4), which undercuts the necessity of the full spectral (SVD-based) transformation and suggests the contribution may reduce to generic gradient normalization.

Novelty concerns: gradient/activation whitening, spectral normalization, and natural-gradient variants are well-established; the main methodological novelty is the specific application to grokking, which is an incremental contribution.

The theory is confined to a linear model with quadratic loss; the jump from 'accelerated convergence to the OLS solution in a 2D toy problem' to 'EGD is guaranteed to rapidly grok' for neural networks is not formally established.

No statistical rigor: single-run curves appear to be shown with no error bars, seeds, or variance reporting, even though grokking dynamics are notoriously sensitive to initialization and hyperparameters.

Computational cost is not quantified: per-step SVD of layer gradient matrices (and pseudo-inverses for rank-deficient stochastic minibatch gradients) could be a substantial overhead; no wall-clock comparisons to SGD or Grokfast are given.

Generalization equivalence is asserted but weakly tested: the paper claims EGD does not compromise final generalization, but only final accuracy on the same toy tasks is shown; data-efficiency, robustness to distribution shift, and effect on learned circuits are not examined.

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming ('EGT' in Fig. 4 caption vs. EGD), lowercase section title ('warm-up'), typos ('proved proved', 'sole due to a delayed convergence least-squares solution'), and text saying EGD is applied 'only on the gradient matrix for the hidden layer' leaves unclear how the method extends to multi-layer or attention architectures.

strengths: The paper is clearly written with a clean narrative: an analytically tractable 2D linear model motivates a spectral normalization of gradients, which is then tested on standard grokking benchmarks (modular arithmetic, sparse parity) and more practical settings (MNIST, transformer on modular arithmetic, non-stationarity on CIFAR-10).

The closed-form analysis of the toy model (Theorems 1-2, plateau length ~ 1/(eta*eps)) is elegant and is empirically validated against the learning curves (Figure 6, Figure 8), which is a nice theory-experiment match.

The connections drawn to natural gradient descent (EGD as whitened NGD), to Grokfast's low-pass filtering bias, and especially to Muon/polar-factor updates are intellectually honest and well contextualized.

The appendix on randomized SVD is useful and practical: it reports both epochs-to-accuracy and wall-clock time, and candidly shows that the simple column-normalization variant is often the best in wall-clock terms.
Hyperparameters, pseudo-code, and the decision to disable EGD once grokking is detected are documented, aiding reproducibility of the experimental setup.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: setting all singular values of the gradient matrix to 1 (the polar factor / orthogonalized update) is essentially what Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) already does via Newton-Schulz iterations, and the paper itself concedes that 'two independently motivated methods converge to a similar geometric operation.' The main new claim is the grokking-acceleration framing, but the mechanistic theory supporting it covers only a 2D linear regression toy problem, not neural networks.

The central causal claim that 'ill-conditioned gradient spectra cause delayed generalization' is supported only by the toy model and correlational evidence (Figure 4). The interaction with weight decay—the standard ingredient in grokking setups and central to competing theories (Omnigrok, weight-norm accounts, circuit efficiency)—is not analyzed theoretically, so the paper does not rule out that EGD mainly alters effective weight norm / regularization dynamics rather than 'equalizing speeds'.

The theory's scope is narrow: linear model, d=2, Gaussian anisotropic data; SGD noise is not treated (only asserted as extendable). There is no convergence or generalization analysis of EGD for even simple MLPs, so the 'effective theory' claimed in the contributions is weaker than advertised.

Some overclaiming: 'guaranteed to drastically grok' is not established beyond the toy model; the 'empirical Fisher' F = GG^T is the gradient outer product, not a Fisher information matrix, and treating its normalization as principled needs care.

Statistical rigor is missing: no error bars, seeds, or distributions of grokking epochs across runs, despite grokking epochs being known to be highly variable. Some hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate 0.7) are unusual and not justified or ablated. The paper does not compare against other strong grokking accelerators beyond Grokfast (e.g., GrokAlign, initialization/norm-based interventions like Omnigrok), which is needed to attribute gains to the spectral mechanism.

Mixed practical results undermine the 'simple, hyperparameter-free' pitch: EGD with exact SVD is unstable on the transformer setting, and wall-clock wins often go to the simple column-normalization heuristic; the randomized SVD rank becomes a tuned hyperparameter in practice.
Reproducibility is incomplete: the code availability footnote is empty (no URL), and variance/seed information is absent.

strengths: The paper is clearly written at a high level and situates itself well in the grokking literature, with a comprehensive related-work section covering mechanistic, kernel-escape, optimization, and delay-mitigation perspectives.

The toy linear model is analytically tractable, and Theorem 1/Corollary 1 plus the equi-distribution analysis in Appendix A.3 provide a clean, closed-form account of how covariance ill-conditioning can produce arbitrarily long plateaus (k* ≍ 1/(ηε)), with reasonable empirical verification (Figure 8).

The core method is simple and well-motivated at the geometric level: replacing the gradient matrix by its polar factor equalizes progress across singular directions, and the paper is honest in deriving its connections to natural gradient descent, Grokfast, and Muon.

Experiments cover the standard grokking benchmarks (modular addition/multiplication, sparse parity) and include wall-clock comparisons against Grokfast using the official Grokfast codebase and hyperparameters, plus RSVD variants that address per-step cost.
The hyperparameter tables, pseudo-code, and additional experiments (MNIST, transformer, non-stationarity on CIFAR-10) support reproducibility of the experimental setup in the main text.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: EGD, G̃ = (GG^T)^{-1/2}G, is essentially an orthogonalized/polar update of the gradient matrix, which the paper itself concedes is the same geometric operation as the Muon optimizer (Section 4.3). The delta over Muon (and over Shampoo/NGD-style preconditioning) is mainly the application domain (grokking) and the use of SVD instead of Newton-Schulz iterations, which is an implementation detail rather than a conceptual advance.

Large theory–practice gap: the 'effective theory' covers only a 2D linear model with quadratic loss on a hand-crafted, contrived data distribution (train data conditioned on |z^T e1| ≥ s, test data conditioned on (z^T v)z^{(1)} ≤ 0). Nothing in the theory applies to MLPs, transformers, modular arithmetic, or parity—the actual experimental settings. Claims such as 'guaranteed to drastically grok' and 'an effective theory' are substantially stronger than the evidence; on the real tasks, the causal link between ill-conditioned gradient spectra and delayed generalization rests on a correlational histogram (Figure 4), and confounders (weight decay, initialization scale, circuit competition) are not ruled out.

The 'hyperparameter-free' selling point is overstated and partially self-refuting: (i) the method must be switched off once a validation accuracy threshold λ is reached (Algorithm 1), introducing a hyperparameter; (ii) the practical RSVD variant requires tuning the rank, which the appendix explicitly states is 'crucial in practice' with task-dependent optimal ranks (128, 40, 30, 36 across tasks); (iii) exact SVD is up to ~14x slower per epoch than vanilla SGD.

Stability problems undermine the practical claim: the paper's own Figure 14 shows EGD with exact SVD leads to 'extremely unstable training' on the modular multiplication transformer task, only being rescued by the RSVD variant. A proposed optimizer that is catastrophically unstable in one of its showcase settings is a significant unresolved issue.

The trivial Column Normalization baseline is embarrassingly competitive: it often achieves the best wall-clock time to 95% accuracy (Tables 2, 3, and best in two of three cases) and groks dramatically faster than vanilla SGD. This suggests the phenomenon is driven by a coarse normalization effect rather than the carefully derived equalization of singular values, weakening the paper's central mechanistic narrative. In one setting (parity k=4) column normalization fails entirely, and the paper does not diagnose why.

Evaluation rigor is thin: no error bars, no multiple seeds, and learning curves appear to be single runs. For grokking, where transition times are notoriously high-variance across seeds, this is a serious omission. Baselines beyond Grokfast (e.g., Omnigrok init-scaling, weight-decay tuning, other accelerators like GrokAlign) are absent.
Reproducibility of code is not actually delivered: the footnote promises 'Code available at' but the link is empty in the submitted manuscript.

Presentation issues further hurt the paper: inconsistent naming ('Egalitarian' vs 'Equalitarian' in the conclusion), garbled Table 4 caption ('reporting epochs to 95time (in milliseconds)'), typos ('los curvae', 'Mudolo Multiplication', 'sup-space'), and a spurious citation to the transformer experiments suggesting EGD is 'effective... also in improving adaptability' that contradicts the admitted instability.

The mechanistic contribution to understanding grokking is limited: the toy model's grokking is really just slow convergence of an ill-conditioned linear least-squares problem—Insight #1 admits the profile is 'solely due to a delayed convergence to the least-squares solution.' Whether this speaks to grokking in overparameterized networks with weight decay and memorization/generalization circuit competition remains speculative.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a clean and understandable core idea: replacing each layer's gradient matrix by its polar factor (normalized singular directions) so that all principal directions evolve at equal speed.

The toy linear model in Section 3 is analytically tractable and yields a closed-form characterization of the plateau length (Theorems 1–2, Corollary 1), and the theory is empirically validated (Figures 6 and 8), which is more rigor than most grokking-acceleration papers provide.

The empirical evaluation is broad: modular addition/multiplication for several moduli, sparse parity with several (n,k), MNIST with MLP/AdamW, modular arithmetic with a 2-layer transformer/Adam, plus wall-clock time and per-epoch cost analysis with randomized SVD, comparisons to Grokfast, a non-stationarity study, and trajectory diagnostics.

The paper honestly reports trade-offs (e.g., SVD overhead, instability of exact-SVD EGD on the transformer, failure of the column-normalization variant on parity k=4), and provides pseudo-code and hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility.
The connections drawn to natural gradient descent (Eq. 13), Grokfast (Eq. 14), and Muon are useful for placing the method in the literature.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core operator. The EGD update G→(GG^T)^{-1/2}G is exactly the orthogonalized/polar gradient, which is the same update geometry targeted by Muon (acknowledged in Section 4.3) and closely related to whitened/orthogonal gradient methods. The paper's main distinction is motivation (grokking) rather than the mechanism itself, and no empirical comparison against Muon or Newton-Schulz orthogonalization is provided, despite Muon being the obvious strong baseline.

Gap between theory and claims. The theory ('guaranteed to drastically grok') applies only to a 2D linear regression toy model; no convergence or grokking analysis exists for neural networks. The claim that ill-conditioned gradient spectra cause grokking on modular arithmetic/parity is supported only by correlational evidence (Figure 4 histograms), not by a mechanistic demonstration that this is the operative cause on those tasks.

Practicality concerns undermine the 'simple, hyperparameter-free' framing: exact-SVD EGD is unstable on the transformer setting (Figure 14), and the randomized-SVD variant requires tuning the rank (contradicting the hyperparameter-free claim); on the transformer, EGD with RSVD only matches, and EGD with exact SVD underperforms, Grokfast (Table 7).

Missing ablations and statistical rigor: no error bars/multiple seeds are reported for the headline results; sensitivity of results to weight decay (a known driver of grokking), learning rate, and initialization scale on the real tasks is not systematically studied.

Several presentation defects: the footnote 'Code available at' is empty; the sentence describing the simplified EGD variant on page 9 is cut off mid-sentence ('where we replace each column of G.'); typos ('Equalitarian' vs. 'Egalitarian', 'sup-space', 'Mudolo Multiplication'), and a partially garbled Table 4 caption.

The signature contribution (faster grokking) is demonstrated mostly on small algorithmic tasks with small models; the significance of removing plateaus on these tasks, versus simply reaching the same final solution faster, could be better justified, especially given Appendix F shows EGD converges to different regions of parameter space than vanilla SGD, which is left unexplained.
